title: Jayadeva Gosvami
html:
The Poet Whose Song the Lord Relished

Sri Jayadeva lived three centuries before Mahaprabhu appeared and was not His companion in Navadvipa or Puri. Yet during the final twelve years of His lila the Lord relished, by day and by night, his “Sri Gita-govinda,” and Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura preserved a tradition according to which Mahaprabhu, long before His own appearance, revealed His golden form to the poet. For this reason one of the biographies of the Lord's associates begins with him. He is called Sri Jayadeva and Jayadeva Gosvami, and under this name the Vaishnava calendar of Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math observes the day of his departure. One of the biographies, in the words of the poem itself, also calls him “Jayadeva Sarasvati.”1

The same biography opens its account with an interpretation of the name itself. Jaya here is He who surpasses all, Sri Krishna, and deva comes from the verb “to reveal, to illumine”: Jayadeva is the one who by the power of his bhakti reveals Krishna to the world.2 So a poet-devotee discloses the Lord to others: his song leads to Krishna.

Time and Homeland

Opinions differ as to when he lived. According to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in the “Anubhashya,” some place him in the eleventh or twelfth Shaka century, and the biographies repeat this. One thing is certain: he lived under Lakshmana Sena, king of Bengal, that is, in the twelfth century, some three hundred years before Mahaprabhu appeared.3 The day of his appearance is not in our calendar, nor do the sources give it.

Nor is there agreement about his birthplace. Most hold that his birthplace was Kendubilva (Kenduli), a village of Birbhum; others name Utkala (Orissa), still others the south of India. The “Anubhashya” lists the same three opinions. Kendubilva lies by the river Ajay, twenty miles south of Suri. Here, it is said, his parents lived: his father, Sri Bhojadeva, and Vamadevi, his mother.

With this river is linked the tradition of his Deities. Sri Radha-Madhava, whom he served all his life, Jayadeva, as the tradition tells, found in the waters of the Ajay. And on the bank of the same river, at the shrine of Shiva Kuleshvara, he would, it is said, rest and perform his bhajana.4

At the Court of Lakshmana Sena

For many years Jayadeva made his home in Navadvipa, then the capital of Bengal, on the bank of the Ganga, not far from the royal palace. He was a court pandita, a poet, of Lakshmana Sena. The foremost scholar of the court was Govardhana Acharya; the dictionary of Ashutosh Deb also calls Jayadeva a court poet of Lakshmana Sena. In the “Gita-govinda” Jayadeva himself names other poets of that court — Sri Umapatidhara, Acharya Sri Govardhana and the one he honours as “king of poets” (kavi-kshmapati); all were great poets and his friends.5

Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Navadvipa-dhama-mahatmya” tells how Lakshmana Sena came to know of him. While Jayadeva was living near the palace, the king heard his “Dashavatara-stotra,” the hymn to the Lord's ten avataras, and was amazed. Govardhana Acharya revealed to him who the author was. Then the king, laying aside his royal robes, came to the poet unrecognized; finding in him every mark of a mahatma, he grew still more attached to him, revealed who he was, and begged him to live in the palace.

Jayadeva had no interest in worldly grandeur. He refused, saying he meant to leave for Purushottama, for Puri. The king entreated him to stay in Navadvipa and offered him for his bhajana the village of Champahati in Navadvipa-mandala; formerly it was called Champaka-hatta, after a grove of champaka trees and a market where their flowers were sold. There the king built him a hut and humbly promised never to come to him without his leave.

The Golden Form at Champahati

At Champahati, according to the testimony of the same Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura, Jayadeva received what makes him honoured among the associates of Gaura. Once, in this very place, back in the Satya-yuga, Dvija Vaninatha had seen the Lord in a form the colour of champaka.6 So too Jayadeva first beheld Sri Radha and Govinda, and then Mahaprabhu, Their united form, golden like a champaka flower.7 This is theologically exact: Sri Chaitanya is Krishna Himself, who has taken the feelings and lustre of Radha — Radha and Krishna become One:

“Sri Radha is the transformation of Krishna's love, His pleasure potency, hladini-shakti. Therefore, though Radha and Krishna are one in Self, from time without beginning They have appeared in the world in two different forms. Now these Two have become one and are manifest as Sri Chaitanya. I bow to Him, Krishna Himself, adorned with the sentiment and the lustre of Sri Radha.” (CC, Adi 1.5)

Having revealed Himself, Mahaprabhu sent him to Purushottama. Showing His champaka-coloured form, the Lord disclosed the future: He would appear in Navadvipa, accept sannyasa, come to Puri and there relish his “Gita-govinda.” Jayadeva obeyed, though separation from Navadvipa-dhama, where his Lord was one day to appear, tormented him.

Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura also writes that the mood of Sri Gaurangadeva awakened within pure devotees' hearts even before He openly appeared in the world: in the hearts of Jayadeva, Bilvamangala, Chandidasa and Vidyapati. Their writings are full of that very understanding of bhakti which Mahaprabhu later brought. That is why the Lord relished their songs: in them sounded His own bhava.

The “Gita-govinda”

The “Sri Gita-govinda,” known too as the “Ashtapadi,” Jayadeva composed, according to these traditions, already in Sri Jagannatha-kshetra, in Puri.8 It is a transcendental poem of separation, vipralambha-rasa. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes of it in the “Anubhashya”:

“His book of poetry is called the ‘Gita-govinda,’ or ‘Ashtapadi.’ It too abounds in transcendental vipralambha-rasa. It describes the vipralambha-rasa that nourishes the rasa of sambhoga — the separation that arose when the prince of Vraja left the place of the rasa dance, as the ‘Srimad-Bhagavatam’ tells.” (“Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 13.42)

The hymn to the ten avataras that so amazed Lakshmana Sena is held by one of the biographies to be part of the “Gita-govinda” itself (dashavatara-gita); others name it separately, without saying whether it belongs to the poem.

Old books, too, bear witness to the poet's time. One of the biographies cites them from the preface to a Calcutta edition of the “Gita-govinda”: in the “Alankara-shekhara,” written by order of King Manikya Chandra before the Muslim conquest of Delhi, Jayadeva is named as a poet at the court of Orissa's king; Shridhara Dasa, son of one of Lakshmana Sena's chief ministers, took many of his verses into the anthology “Sad-ukti-karnamrita,” referring to a certain work (in the text, “Amiyabha-kavya”); and the colophon of one ancient manuscript says that Jayadeva was famed as a poet in the time of Lakshmana Sena.

For whom this song is meant Jayadeva said himself, at its very beginning:

“If your mind finds rasa in remembering Hari, if it is curious about the art of His pastimes, then listen to the speech of Jayadeva, a garland of sweet, tender and lovely words.” (“Gita-govinda” 1.3)9

And again, at the close of one of the songs: “While Sri Jayadeva, serving Hari, sings this most charming song, bow down to Hari — joyful, supremely kind, beloved of the virtuous.” (“Gita-govinda,” song 11)10 The poem discloses the intimate pastimes of Sri Radha and Govinda, full of shringara-rasa — madhurya-rasa, the highest sweetness of love for Krishna — and only the fortunate, who have sukriti, spiritual merit, and a longing to remember Hari, are fit to serve it. This is not mundane love poetry: shringara is the highest rasa of pure bhakti, and to measure it by a worldly standard is an offence.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta says this plainly. The feelings that blossomed in Chandidasa, Vidyapati and Jayadeva were Mahaprabhu's most beloved delicacy; but only the most fortunate person can follow them, one indifferent both to enjoyment and to renunciation who eternally longs to serve Sri Radha. Lovers of mundane poetry and the sect of the prakrita-sahajiyas, fancying themselves “raganuga,” impudently take up these songs, and as a result licentiousness and atheism grow in the world, and they themselves are led to hell:

“Unqualified people, who take the body for the self, are full of thirst for what is unworthy and burdened with anarthas, may take the supramundane pastimes of Sri Radha and Krishna, worshipped by the supremely liberated, to be the tasteless, vile amorous sports of a mundane hero and heroine, or something like them — and end up gratifying their senses. Therefore any kind of discussion of the pastimes of Radha and Krishna is strictly forbidden to them.” (“Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 13.42)

The secret of the poem is revealed in its very first lines. One of the biographies gives an interpretation of the word “by night” (naktam) in the first verse (meghair meduram ambaram…): by it Jayadeva pointed to the hour at the end of the night when Radha and Krishna are joined in an inseparable embrace and assume one form — the form of Sri Gaurasundara; and at this very hour, the same biography says, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati left the world.11

The “Gita-govinda” had long been known. When Srila Rupa Gosvami gathered the scattered verses of Vaishnava poets in the “Padyavali,” he noted specially in its conclusion that he had not included verses from the works of Jayadeva, Vishvamangala and others: the “Gita-govinda” already circulated as a whole book. And the twenty-one songs of Ramananda Raya's “Jagannatha-vallabha-nataka” closely resemble the songs of the “Gita-govinda.” Narahari Chakravarti in the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” describing how Raghava Pandita of Govardhana showed Srinivasa Dhira-samira on the bank of the Yamuna — the place of the wondrous meeting of Radha and Krishna — quotes verses of the “Gita-govinda” with the refrain “Where the gentle breeze blows on the bank of the Yamuna, in the forest, Vanamali waits” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 5.2374–2378).

Padmavati

From his youth Jayadeva was detached from the world and had no thought of marriage; and yet, by the Lord's will, he had to accept the virtuous Padmavati as his wife. The tradition tells it thus. Her father, a brahmana, at Jagannatha's command came with the girl to Jayadeva, begging him to marry her. When Jayadeva would not, the brahmana left her there and went away, and Jayadeva told her she was free to go where she pleased. By another account, a childless brahmana had prayed to Jagannatha for many years for a son, but a daughter was born — Padmavati; when she grew up, her father brought her to give her to Jagannatha Himself, and the Lord told him: “I have a servant, Jayadeva, who has left his home and sings My names. Give her to him.” Jayadeva for his part offered to take the girl wherever she might say.12

Padmavati humbly replied: “By Jagannatha's will my father has given me to you. You alone will I choose as my husband; I will accept no other and will never break faith. Even if you abandon me, I will not abandon you and will always serve your feet.”13 Jayadeva had no other way, and he accepted her. So the detached devotee became a householder — not by yielding to the world, but by fulfilling the will of the Lord, who Himself gave him a devotee-wife so that together they might serve Him.

The Line Written by Krishna

Jayadeva installed a Deity of Narayana, and a river of Krishna-prema began to flow in his heart; in its waves he was writing the “Gita-govinda.” One day, the tradition tells, he was writing the song in which Krishna appeases the angry Radha — the one that begins “if You speak even a little…” (vadasi yadi kinchid api) — and came to the line: “Place on My head as an ornament Your generous foot, tender as a shoot: it removes the poison of Kamadeva” (smara-garala-khandanam mama shirasi mandanam dehi pada-pallavam udaram, “Gita-govinda” 10.8). But Jayadeva did not dare to write that Sri Krishna places Radha's foot on His own head. Leaving the song unfinished, he went to bathe.14

Soon Padmavati saw Jayadeva come back, write something in the manuscript, take his meal and leave again. While she was taking what he had left, the real Jayadeva came in and asked in surprise: “Why do you eat today ahead of me?” Padmavati answered that he had already eaten and gone, and before that had written something in the book. Jayadeva looked into the manuscript — and there were the missing words “dehi pada-pallavam udaram” in his own handwriting, and the ink was not yet dry. He understood: these words had been written, and the song completed, by Sri Krishna Himself, the foremost relisher of rasa. His hair stood on end, and tears streamed down his face.15 This tradition is kept by the “Sri Rasika-mangala” as well: its very first verse says that there are many Puranas and Itihasas in the world, but nowhere except in the “Gita-govinda” did Krishna Himself write anything with His own hand.

In a trembling voice he said to Padmavati: “Most fortunate are you: Sri Krishna Himself has given you His darshana, and you are honouring His prasada. I was not so blessed. I too will take your remnants” — and he ate what she had left. One of the biographies adds that this tradition is generally accepted as authentic.

Jayadeva's hesitation was no weakness of faith: it was reverence (aishvarya-jnana), which does not dare to describe the Lord of all at Radha's feet. But Krishna writes this line Himself, because He is conquered by the love of Radha, the highest of His devotees; this is no lessening of God, but the sway of pure prema over Him. And that Jayadeva took the remnants of his wife's meal is no breach of custom, but the humility of a Vaishnava who recognized that she had received a mercy he himself had not.

Jagannatha Listens to the “Gita-govinda”

In Puri another tradition is kept. A woman of the gardeners' caste (malini) used to sing the “Gita-govinda,” wholly lost in its mood. Attracted by her song, Jagannatha would come there, listen as long as she sang, and return to the temple. One day the king of Utkala, coming for darshana, saw dust on Jagannatha's body and thorns in His cloth. The pujari-pandas could not explain it and were frightened. That night Jagannatha appeared in the king's dream and told him that no one was at fault: He had gone to the gardener-woman to hear the “Gita-govinda,” and there, in the garden, dust and thorns had caught on Him.

Then the king sent a palanquin for her and had her sing the poem in Jagannatha's presence. Ever since, the women of her family sing this poem daily in the temple before the Lord, and the devotees of Puri call them not gardener-women but devadasis, servants of the Deity. So, according to the tradition, began the singing of the “Gita-govinda” for Jagannatha. Jagannatha is Krishna Himself, not an image: the dust and the thorns that clung to Him are the play of the Lord, who is drawn by the song of His devotee. The singing of a devadasi was later heard by Mahaprabhu as well; this is told below.

The Lord Thatches the Roof

Many wonders are told of Jayadeva. With deep love he served Sri Radha-Madhava. Once, in the scorching heat, he was laying straw on the roof of his hut, and someone below was handing him ropes and bundles of straw so that the work would go faster. Jayadeva thought it was Padmavati, but on coming down he learned that she had been doing other work all the while. Entering the temple, he saw that Radha-Madhava's hands were covered with soot and dirt, understood who had helped him, fell before Them and wept.16 As the devotee is devoted to the Lord, so the Lord is devoted to His devotee.

The Robbers

To raise funds for the worship and festivals of his life's treasure, Radha-Madhava, Jayadeva travelled to other lands, where his poetic gift brought him offerings. On the way back robbers fell upon him: they robbed him, hacked off his hands and feet and cast him down a well. Enduring terrible pain, he loudly repeated the name of Hari.

Three days later a king was hunting nearby. Hearing the name of Hari from the well, he was amazed, had the wounded Jayadeva drawn out, brought him to the palace and surrounded him with care; through the efforts of the king and queen he gradually recovered. Recognizing in him a great devotee and listening to his sweet rendering of the “Gita-govinda,” the king brought Padmavati to the palace as well. The royal couple accepted initiation in the Vishnu-mantra17 and lived listening to Jayadeva speak of Krishna and serving the Vaishnavas.

One day those very robbers came to the palace disguised as Vaishnavas. Jayadeva recognized them but had them received with every honour. Not understanding his noble intent and fearing exposure and punishment, they hurried away without taking the hospitality offered. Seeing that they were afraid, Jayadeva had the king present them with much money and send escorts with them. When they had gone a little way, the robbers told the escorts: “No need to go further. But tell your king in secret: we used to serve another king, and for some reason he commanded us to put your mahanta-babaji to death. We hacked off his hands and feet. He is afraid the secret will come out — that is why he had us given money and quickly sent away.”

Mother Earth could not bear this lie, and the robbers wondrously sank into the ground. For, as the “Bhagavatam” says:

“The Earth spoke thus: ‘There is no unrighteousness greater than falsehood. I can bear everything — only not a man given to falsehood.’” (“Srimad-Bhagavatam” 8.20.4)

These words are spoken by Bali in answer to Shukracharya, who was dissuading him from his gift to Vamanadeva.

The king's servants, who had seen the wondrous punishment that befell the offenders at the feet of a mahabhagavata, related the whole matter to the king from beginning to end. At the king's questioning, Jayadeva related what had happened to him on the road and said: “Sadhus do not take revenge on those who wrong them, but try to satisfy them with courtesy. Yet by the inexorable law of the Lord they had to taste the fruit of their deeds.” The sadhu forgives, but an offence at the feet of a great devotee the Lord does not leave without its consequence.

Padmavati's Test

Padmavati and the queen became close friends. In those days there was the custom of sati, in which a widow ascended her husband's funeral pyre. Once, when the queen was grieving that the widow of her brother was to ascend the pyre, Padmavati said to her: “When the husband leaves the world, the life of a faithful wife does not remain in the body.”

Wishing to put this to the test, one day the queen announced to Padmavati that Jayadeva had left his body. The moment she heard it, the faithful Padmavati herself left her body. The queen, thinking herself guilty, sobbed, and the king in tears earnestly begged Jayadeva to restore his wife's life. Jayadeva let the nectar of Krishna's name flow into Padmavati's ears — and she came back to herself, as if awakening from sleep. Seeing the wondrous greatness of both, the whole royal family with the king and queen bowed again and again at the feet of Jayadeva and Padmavati. The power of this miracle lies in the holy name sounding from the lips of a great devotee; and in Padmavati's departure the tradition sees an image of the perfect fidelity of a wife wholly given to her Vaishnava husband.

In Vrindavana

Then Jayadeva was drawn to Vrindavana. He bade farewell to the king and queen and, carrying his beloved Sri Radha-Madhava, set out. In Vrindavana he served Them at Keshi-tirtha, the Keshi-ghata on the Yamuna. Hearing how sweetly he sang the “Gita-govinda,” the residents of the dhama lost all outer awareness. A certain mahajana, a wealthy merchant, raised a temple for his Radha-Madhava over Keshi-ghata.

Last Years and Departure

Where Jayadeva spent his last days the traditions disagree: according to some, in Jagannatha-kshetra; according to others, in Vrindavana; according to still others, in his native Kendubilva. According to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Gosvami Prabhupada, his last years were passed in Jagannatha-kshetra; so he writes in the “Anubhashya” as well: “He spent the last part of his life at Sri Jagannatha-kshetra.” This is the view we follow.18

Another tradition says that after long years in Vrindavana Jayadeva went back to Kendubilva and performed his bhajana there. For his bath in the Ganga he had to walk a long way every day. Once it so happened that he could not go, and he grew very sad — and then the goddess Ganga herself flowed to Kendubilva and bestowed her mercy on him. According to this tradition, it was there, in his homeland, that his pastimes as a sadhaka came to a close; in his memory a fair, the Jayadeva-mela, is held at Kendubilva every year to this day, on Magha-sankranti.19

But if he did end his days in Kendubilva, it was without his Deities: nowhere is it said that he brought Them to his homeland. When he had disappeared from view, the king of Jaipur removed Sri Radha-Madhava, whose service was dearer to him than life, and installed Them at Ghati; in Jaipur They are served still.

He left this world on krishna-shashthi, the sixth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pausha. In our calendar this is Madhava-masa, krishna-shashthi; in 2026 the day of his departure fell on 9 January, and in 2027 it falls on 28 January.20

Mahaprabhu Relishes the “Gita-govinda”

Jayadeva's song sounds in the “Charitamrita” from the Lord's early pastimes to the last. Already in Navadvipa, having defeated the digvijayi Keshava Kashmiri in debate, the young Nimai consoles the poet by saying that flaws are found even in the greatest:

“Even in the poetry of Bhavabhuti, Jayadeva and Kalidasa faults appear.” (CC, Adi 16.101)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” on this verse refers the reader to his account of Jayadeva at Adi 13.42.

Verses of the “Gita-govinda” sound also in the Lord's conversation with Ramananda Raya on the bank of the Godavari. When Ramananda tells how Krishna left the rasa dance and sorrowfully searched for Radha alone, the “Charitamrita” quotes:

“Placing Radha in His heart — the chain that bound His desire for the very essence of the rasa — Krishna, the enemy of Kamsa, left the other beauties of Vraja.” (CC, Madhya 8.105; “Gita-govinda” 3.1)

It is followed by verse 3.2 — how Krishna, full of remorse, searched for Radha and sank down in despair in a grove on the bank of the Yamuna (Madhya 8.106); and the spring song of the “Gita-govinda” (1.11) — “Friend, see how Sri Hari sports in spring!” — the “Charitamrita” quotes in the same conversation (Madhya 8.143), and earlier still at Adi 4.224. Verse 3.1 appears also at Adi 4.219; there Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that Krishna left the place of the rasa and went to seek Radha, the chief shelter of the rasa. Verse 3.2 he quotes also in the “Anubhashya” on Madhya 17.216: when Radha is not near, Krishna, who enchants the universe, is Himself enchanted by Madana — as the “Gita-govinda” says: “Having searched for Radhika everywhere, His heart tormented by the wounds of Ananga's arrows…”

When Svarupa Damodara came to Puri, the Lord gained one who knew His heart. Krishnadasa Kaviraja writes:

“Anything contrary to the conclusions of bhakti, or any rasabhasa (a mere semblance of rasa), brought the Lord's heart no delight when He heard it. Therefore Svarupa Gosani examined everything, and only if it was pure did he let the Lord hear it. With the songs of Vidyapati and Chandidasa and the ‘Sri Gita-govinda’ — these three — he delighted the Lord.” (CC, Madhya 10.113–115)

Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” calls the “Sri Gita-govinda” the famous poem of Sri Jayadeva, full of Sanskrit songs of krishna-rasa.

Above all the Lord relished it in His last twelve years, when, steeped in the bhava of Radha, He lived in the Gambhira in unceasing separation from Krishna:

“Just as Sri Radha raved on seeing Uddhava, so He raved in His divine madness night and day. With Ramananda and Svarupa He relished the songs of Vidyapati, Jayadeva and Chandidasa.” (CC, Adi 13.41–42)

“With Svarupa and Ramananda, Mahaprabhu night and day sang and heard the songs of Chandidasa and Vidyapati, Raya's drama, the ‘Karnamrita’ and the ‘Sri Gita-govinda’ in supreme bliss.” (CC, Madhya 2.77)

In the “Anubhashya” on this verse Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that the “songs” here are the singing of verses of Chandidasa, Vidyapati, Ramananda, Bilvamangala and Jayadeva.21

Svarupa and Ramananda consoled the Lord in His separation:

“Those two consoled the Lord: Svarupa sang songs, and Raya recited verses. With the verses and songs of the ‘Krishna-karnamrita,’ of Vidyapati and of the ‘Sri Gita-govinda’ they gave the Lord joy.” (CC, Antya 15.26–27)

One night the feelings of the gopis who searched for Krishna on the night of the rasa dance awoke in the Lord, and Svarupa sang for Him a verse from the “Gita-govinda”:

“My mind remembers Hari, who here in the rasa dance enjoyed His pastimes and His jests.” (CC, Antya 15.84; “Gita-govinda” 2.3)22

So it was day after day:

“Whatever feeling arose in the Lord, Svarupa Mahashaya would sing a song to suit it. And Raya Ramananda would recite verses suited to His feelings from Vidyapati, Chandidasa and the ‘Sri Gita-govinda.’” (CC, Antya 17.5–6)

And on one such night, when the Lord, returning for a moment to outer consciousness, asked, “Svarupa, sing something sweet,” Svarupa sang songs of Vidyapati and of the “Gita-govinda,” and they soothed Mahaprabhu's ears (Antya 17.62).23

A song of the “Gita-govinda” once nearly drew the Lord through a thorny thicket. Walking to the temple of Yameshvara, He heard a devadasi singing the “Gita-govinda” in the raga gurjari and, forgetting everything, ran towards the voice, unaware of the thorns piercing His body; His servant Govinda managed to hold Him back (Antya 13.78–88). Another time, roaming the Jagannatha-vallabha garden, the Lord had His associates sing the spring song of the “Gita-govinda,” “Lalita-lavanga- lata,” and danced to it (Antya 19.84). Govinda-deva tells something similar in the “Gaura-krishnodaya”: once in spring, seeing the beauty of a wondrous garden, the Lord in rapture described it with verses of the “Gita-govinda” (18.5).

And at the very end of the “Charitamrita,” summing up the Lord's last pastimes, Krishnadasa Kaviraja writes:

“Whatever verses of Jayadeva, of the ‘Bhagavata,’ of Ramananda Raya's drama and of the ‘Karnamrita’ suited each mood, He would recite in that mood and relish, absorbed in that emotion.” (CC, Antya 20.67–68)

The verses of “Jayadeva” here, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains, are his ashtapadi songs, that is, the “Gita-govinda.” And the “Gaura-krishnodaya” names the songs of the “Gita-govinda” among what Gaura, having taken it into His heart, constantly recited within during His last twelve years (18.13).

His Memory Among the Gaudiya Vaishnavas

Jayananda at the beginning of his “Chaitanya-mangala,” listing the poets who sang of the Lord before him, writes: “Jayadeva, Vidyapati and Chandidasa — they revealed the deeds of Sri Krishna.” Later generations of devotees too honoured Jayadeva's poem; the “Karnananda” says that Srinivasa Acharya at Yajigram sang the “Sri Gita-govinda,” the songs of Chandidasa and Vidyapati and Raya's drama in supreme bliss. The commentary “Krishna-vallabha” on the “Krishna-karnamrita,” known under the name of Gopala Bhatta Gosvami, quotes the “Gita-govinda”; among the works of Prabodhananda Sarasvati a commentary on it is also named. In the “Pada-kalpataru” of Vaishnava Dasa there is a song, “Sri Jayadeva-vandana,” signed with the name “dasa Raghunatha”: it glorifies the merciful Jayadeva, beloved of Padmavati, who composed the sweet “Gita-govinda” — he whose form is the very rasa of love for Radha-Madhava and whose beautiful abode is Kendubilva; and it glorifies the feet of Padmavati as well.24

Significance

Jayadeva was not, in the narrow sense, a companion of the Lord in His earthly pastimes. He belongs to those pure devotees in whose hearts, in the words of Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura, the bhava of Gaura lived even before His appearance; and the Lord, when He came, relished their songs as His own innermost treasure. His poem is not mundane lyric but a song of the transcendental separation and union of Radha and Govinda, and Mahaprabhu, Krishna Himself in the mood of Radha, listened to it in the Gambhira to His last days.

Jayadeva's own life, as the traditions preserve it, is a lesson in bhakti. His name is explained as “the one who reveals Krishna”; the Lord completes his song and thatches the roof of his hut, because He is devoted to His devotee. Maimed, in a well, he repeats the name of Hari; he answers those who wronged him with honour; and the name of Krishna on his lips brings Padmavati back to life. But the “Gita-govinda,” as he himself warns and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta after him, opens only to those whose hearts long to remember Hari and to serve Sri Radha.
